summary: Misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin E1 analog used to prevent NSAID-induced gastric ulcers by increasing mucosal bicarbonate/mucus production and reducing acid secretion. It carries a boxed warning: given to pregnant women it can cause uterine rupture, abortion, premature birth, or birth defects, and it is contraindicated in pregnancy. Patients must be warned of its abortifacient property and told not to give it to others.
indications: Prevention of NSAID-induced gastric ulcers in patients at high risk of ulcer complications
Gastric mucosal protection in patients requiring chronic NSAID therapy

moa: Misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) analog with gastric antisecretory and mucosal protective properties. NSAIDs deplete mucosal prostaglandins, reducing bicarbonate and mucus secretion; misoprostol restores these protective effects and, at doses of 200 mcg and above, also inhibits gastric acid secretion by binding prostaglandin receptors on parietal cells. Its prostaglandin activity also stimulates uterine contraction, accounting for its abortifacient effect.

preg: CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy. Administration of misoprostol to pregnant women can cause uterine rupture, abortion, premature birth, or birth defects; uterine rupture has occurred when misoprostol was used to induce labor or abortion. Congenital anomalies, sometimes with fetal death, have been reported after unsuccessful use as an abortifacient. If a patient becomes pregnant, discontinue and advise of the risks to her and the fetus.
lact: The active metabolite misoprostol acid may be present in breast milk and could cause diarrhea in a breastfed infant; breastfeeding is generally not recommended during treatment. Weigh the benefits of breastfeeding against the mother's need and potential infant risk.
renal: No routine dose adjustment is required; the dose may be reduced (e.g. to 100 mcg) if the standard dose is not tolerated.
hepatic: No routine dose adjustment is required; misoprostol is metabolized by fatty-acid oxidizing systems rather than hepatic microsomal enzymes.

missed: Take the missed dose with food as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose; do not take two doses at once.
overdose: The toxic dose in humans has not been established; cumulative daily doses up to 1600 mcg have been tolerated with only GI discomfort. Signs of overdose may include sedation, tremor, convulsions, dyspnea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, palpitations, hypotension, or bradycardia. Treat with supportive and symptomatic care; there is no specific antidote.
